title: From Experience to Memory: Learning, Plasticity, and Recall
kicker: Learning Systems, Memory Circuits, and Lasting Synaptic Change
takeaways: Learning changes several interacting memory systems.
Conditioned responses, skills, perceptual familiarity, and relational memories can change independently; improvement does not always require conscious recollection.
Hippocampal circuits represent relationships and context.
Place coding, ensemble activity, and human amnesia show separable contributions to encoding and richly detailed retrieval rather than one universal memory store.
Hippocampal ripples, cortical activity, inhibition, and experience influence memory over time; older episodic details can still depend on hippocampal integrity.
Retrieval can preserve or modify what is remembered.
Recall depends on cues and ensemble access, and repeated retrieval can alter later competition or updating; failure to express a memory need not prove its erasure.
Synaptic strengthening has identifiable cellular steps.
Coincident activity can permit NMDA-dependent calcium entry, activate enzymes, alter AMPA receptor delivery, and change dendritic spine structure.
Lasting memory is more than one molecular switch.
Trafficking, actin, inhibitory circuits, protein synthesis, and compensating pathways contribute at different times; a synaptic assay and a remembered event are distinct measurements.
